images.caption: Figure 1:Coding agents as visual reasoners.Given the same first frame and prompt, a video generation model denoises the answer video directly, whereas a coding agent writes and executes a program that renders it. Both outputs share one video format and are scored by the same unmodified official evaluator, which compares them against symbolic ground truth using classical computer vision. The coding agent outperforms the best video model overall. The two solutions to one sequence task illustrate how the agents differ: Claude Code navigates the image to recover a transferable scheme (depictive), whereas Codex resolves the specific visual problem by hard-coding the answer it identified for that instance (propositional).

Figure 4:Depictive and propositional programs on the same instance of G-131. (a) The input frame shared by both agents. (b) Claude Code (depictive): the program measures the circle widths, computes the constant difference and evaluates the candidates at run time. (c) Codex (propositional): the correct candidate is identified in the session, and the program only renders and highlights it. Both agents select the same candidate and obtain the same score.

Figure 7:The Codex program for G-13 (grid number sequence task, instance 00000; 3 tool calls, 20 s, score 1.0), shown alongside the task’s first frame and the final frame it renders. The nine corner cells of the route are written into the program as literals derived from the agent’s visual reading of the image, with each leg annotated by its Manhattan length. The sprite is erased from its starting cell and re-stamped pixel-for-pixel at each interpolated position along the route, leaving the board itself unchanged throughout the video.
